cases.abstract: Imitation policies trained on few demonstrations can fail when their own errors carry the robot beyond expert trajectories. DMD expands the supervised training distribution with pose-conditioned diffusion images and corrective actions, rather than relying on appearance augmentation alone. A pretrained view model is adapted using task demonstrations, task-agnostic play, or both to synthesize displaced wrist-camera views. Geometrically derived labels target later expert poses, mitigating backward supervision when a sampled displacement overshoots the next frame. Physical experiments cover pushing, stacking, pouring, and shirt hanging. With 24 apple-pushing demonstrations and ten trials per method, DMD reaches 100% success, compared with 30% for behavior cloning and 50% for a replicated NeRF-based augmentation method. With eight demonstrations and a play-trained view model, success is 80%, versus 20% for behavior cloning. Beyond scarce-data learning, augmentation improves a diffusion policy from 4/25 to 16/25 successful cup arrangements after training on 1,447 demonstrations and testing unseen cups in an unseen environment; both policies use cropped, rectified images. The approach assumes that generated states remain recoverable, which excludes reversing events such as spilled contents.
cases.methods: DMD couples a synthesized observation to a geometrically defined recovery action, so an off-trajectory image is not left with its original demonstration label. A pretrained latent diffusion model is fine-tuned on image pairs and relative camera transforms reconstructed from task or play trajectories. A sampled local displacement then specifies both the desired wrist-camera view and its virtual camera pose. Composing the inverse displacement with reconstructed expert poses gives the transform from that virtual pose to a future demonstration pose. The next frame is not always a suitable target: a sampled view may already lie beyond it, causing its label to direct retreat rather than progress. Pushing therefore uses the third future frame, where offline angular error approximately plateaus; farther targets also exclude more final trajectory frames. Mixing these labeled examples with real demonstrations supplies supervision for recoverable deviations instead of only the expert path.
cases.results: Diffusion-generated recovery examples improve prediction even when conventional image augmentation is already present: with color jitter and flips, median angular error falls from 0.355 to 0.328 radians. The corresponding apple-pushing policies trained on 24 demonstrations achieve 30% success for behavior cloning and 100% for DMD in ten trials each. The modest improvement in held-out action predictions thus accompanies a much larger change in task completion. Task-only view-model training still gives 80% pushing success, compared with 100% using task and play data, indicating that play is helpful but not required in this setting. In separate randomized pouring comparisons, DMD also outperforms behavior cloning when its view model uses task and play data (80% versus 0%) or task data alone (70% versus 30%). Because those comparisons were conducted separately under potentially different conditions, they do not establish a pouring advantage from play data. The supported benefit is corrective supervision for recoverable departures, not restoration after an irreversible spill.
cases.notes: Retained corrective labeling as the main contribution and cup arrangement as evidence beyond scarce demonstrations. Tables I-II connect appearance-augmentation controls with robot success. Eight-demonstration pushing uses play data for view-model training. Table IV's pouring comparisons are separate randomized tests, not a controlled play-data comparison. Table V uses cropped, rectified images for both retrained policies. Recoverability remains a methodological assumption.

cases.abstract: Fine bimanual manipulation requires precise demonstrations and policies that tolerate errors across long, high-frequency trajectories. ALOHA and Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) address these linked requirements. ALOHA provides an open-source teleoperation system within a USD 20,000 budget, using 50 Hz joint-space leader-follower control to avoid inverse-kinematics failures near singularities. ACT predicts chunks of future joint targets from images and joint observations, shortening the modeled horizon; overlapping predictions are combined at every control step to incorporate feedback and smooth motion. Conditional variational training accommodates variability in human demonstrations. Evaluation covers two simulated and six physical tasks, using 50 demonstrations for most physical tasks and 100 for velcro threading. With one training seed and 25 physical evaluations per method, ACT achieves 88% success opening a slider bag and 96% inserting a battery, while four tuned imitation baselines complete neither task. Ablations support distinct roles for chunking and variational training. A six-person study also finds faster teleoperation at 50 Hz than at 5 Hz. However, velcro threading succeeds in only 20% of trials despite the larger demonstration set, and initial candy-unwrapping evaluation yields no successful completion in ten trials.
cases.methods: Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) predicts future leader-arm joint targets from the follower arms' current joint positions and four camera views. Using leader targets preserves command offsets through which the motor controllers exert force, rather than merely reproducing achieved follower positions. Predicting an action sequence reduces the effective horizon when chunks are executed together, but observing only between chunks would delay feedback and produce abrupt transitions. ACT therefore queries the policy at every control step and averages overlapping predictions for that same execution time with exponential weights. This incorporates observations without mixing actions intended for adjacent times. A conditional variational autoencoder learns a latent style variable from demonstrated sequences and joint observations, allowing reconstruction to represent variation in human behavior under a Gaussian-prior regularizer. At deployment, the encoder is discarded and the latent variable is fixed to zero. The resulting predictions are deterministic while temporal ensembling smooths their execution.
cases.results: The benefit of chunking extends beyond transformers, whereas variational training matters specifically for human demonstrations in the tested simulations. Without temporal ensembling, ACT's mean success across two tasks with scripted or human data rises from 1% for single-step prediction to 44% with 100-step chunks; longer chunks perform slightly worse. BC-ConvMLP and VINN also improve with chunking. Removing conditional variational training barely changes scripted-data performance but lowers the human-data average from 35.3% to 2%. Temporal ensembling is less transferable: separately tuned configurations improve ACT by 3.3 percentage points but reduce VINN from 37% to 17%. Physical outcomes expose remaining difficulties with fine visual alignment: velcro threading reaches 92% at lifting but only 20% at insertion despite 100 demonstrations. Candy unwrapping completes 0/10 initial attempts. A later evaluation unwraps 3/5 candies with ten attempts allowed per candy; the changed retry budget prevents treating this as a directly comparable increase in single-attempt success.
cases.notes: Retained ALOHA and ACT as co-contributions; the high-frequency user study supports the hardware contribution independently of policy success. Figure 9 distinguishes chunking, variational training, and separately tuned temporal-ensemble comparisons. Four-baseline claims apply only to slider-bag opening and battery insertion among physical tasks; the remaining four use BeT. The body specifies L1 reconstruction while Algorithm 1 writes MSE, so no reconstruction metric is asserted. Candy outcomes retain their different retry budgets.
